rv.q: Welcome, if you dare, to the savage world of Anna K. Jacobs and Michael R. Jackson's Teeth , a dark and sharp new musical comedy adapted from Mitchell Lichtenstein's cult 2007 fright flick.
Under Sarah Benson’s claws-out direction, Teeth feels like the musical equivalent of driving a spike-covered Mad Max car across the desert while getting chased by war boys on their way to Valhalla.
Both are fully evident in Sarah Benson’s production, even if they never blend into a satisfying whole.
Jackson and Jacobs have instead created a riotous and prescient vision of where we’re headed as the politics of men and women radically diverge.
Other than this cavity, Teeth has bite.
So even if the message is a little murky, the ride is far too much fun to really care.
Sarah Benson’s direction revels in the grand guignol as it accumulates.

What’s most disappointing about “Teeth” is not its excesses, although these are deliberately in-your-face — the aggressively vulgar lyrics, the gory severed penises – but how the various elements of the show don’t completely hold together.
But even if patrons don’t exit Teeth clamoring for the score on an original cast album, many will appreciate it most of the time, as it hurtles along under Patrick Sulken’s conducting.
Michael R. Jackson and Anna K. Jacobs’s new musical Teeth has bite.
This comical, gross, and over the top battle of slashing and gore personifies the mental process and aftermath of freeing oneself from a wrath.
Nevertheless, it’s a decided improvement over the lackluster original.
There's a sense that the show is following an agenda rather than a well-thought-out narrative structure...

cn.t: Critics find this vagina dentata musical a wild, gleeful satire with sharp performances and catchy songs, though some feel it bites off more than it can chew in tackling sex, shame, and misogyny.
